nestedscales is the core package of a family for multi-level discrete
representations of data, used in modelling, data processing and
visualization. This page lists what the core provides in the current
release, what the dimension packages add, and what is planned. It is updated
with each release.

## Scope

A **nested scale** represents one dimension of a dataset or model as a table
of atoms, the finest units, with one column per coarser level, the frames.
Every frame nests in the atoms. Frames may nest in each other (a tree:
activity in division in section) or overlay each other (hours of the day and
months of the year); every operation routes through the atoms, so both are
handled alike.

The package covers three things:

1. **Structure**: the levels, the units at each level, and which pairs of
   levels nest, cross or are uniform.
2. **Transition rules**: how a value moves between levels -- summed,
   averaged, weighted, copied, or expressed as a share of its parent.
3. **Operations**: converting data, attaching labels, subsetting, combining
   dimensions, grouping units into new levels, and storing data with its
   scales.

## Available now (0.2.0)

### Structure

* `scale_from_leaftable()` builds a scale from a table; `scale_frames()`,
  `scale_units()`, `scale_key()`, `scale_leaftable()`, `scale_weights()`,
  `scale_rank()` and `scale_atom_level()` read it.
* Relations between levels: `scale_nests()`, `scale_crosses()`,
  `scale_is_uniform()`; `scale_family()` and `scale_ancestry()` list
  parent-child pairs; `scale_children()`, `scale_parents()`,
  `scale_descendants()` and `scale_ancestors()` navigate.
* `scale_share()` and `scale_coverage()` report weights and what fraction of
  a parent a subset keeps.
* Partial membership (`NA` at a level) and declared residual units
  (`scale_residuals()`) are part of the representation.
* `filter_scale()` and `prune_scale()` subset and collapse a scale, keeping
  the record of coverage.

### Transition rules

* Seven rules, `SCALE_RULES`: `sum`, `weighted_mean`, `mean`, `copy`, `sd`,
  `share`, `logshare`. Each is defined in both directions, so aggregation
  and disaggregation are one operation.
* Weights are named columns of the scale; several can coexist and each value
  column may use its own.
* `register_scale_rule()` records the rule for a named value column, scoped
  per dimension, so a model's parameters recast without repeating the rule.
* Declared residuals aggregate upward but are never allocated to when a
  coarse value is split.

### Operations

* `recast_scale()` converts data between any two levels of a scale, or to
  the atoms of another scale that shares atom keys; `recast_to_atoms()` and
  `recast_from_atoms()` are its two halves; `recast_crosswalk()` runs the
  same engine over a correspondence built elsewhere.
* `scale_map()` and `scale_map_between()` expose the crosswalks;
  `register_scale_map()` installs exact or hand-audited ones.
* `join_scale()` attaches labels, coarser levels, shares and weights to a
  dataset.
* `reconcile_scale()` compares aggregated data with an independent total and
  can balance the gap.
* `scale_product()` combines several scales into one multi-dimensional
  index; `recast_product()`, `join_product()` and `filter_product()` work
  over it without materialising the product of atoms.
* `cluster_scale()`, `cluster_contiguous()`, `cluster_medoids()` and
  `cluster_sweep()` group units by their data and return the scale with the
  clusters as a new level.
* `as_scale_array()` and `as_scale_table()` move between long tables and
  dense arrays; `write_scale_dataset()` and `open_scale_dataset()` store data
  as a partitioned Arrow dataset together with its scales.
* Every operation accepts a `data.frame`, tibble, `data.table`, dtplyr table
  or arrow dataset and returns the same class; lazy inputs return a query.

### Attributes, aliases and definitions

* A scale may carry **attributes**, physical values keyed by `(frame, unit)`
  at any level (a calorific value on a fuel, on its carrier or on its
  group), each with a `kind`, bounds, unit of measure and source.
  `scale_attributes()` resolves one value per member along the hierarchy
  and says where it came from; `convert_scale()` converts a table row by
  row with it. Attributes are never weights and are never recast.
* **Aliases** are alternative labels per member; `scale_match()` resolves
  labels exactly, case-insensitively, and reports ambiguity.
* **Definition files.** `write_scale()` and `read_scale()` exchange a scale
  as a JSON header with inline tables, or a bundle with Arrow or CSV tables,
  readable by every binding; YAML is accepted. `scale_catalog()` lists the
  definitions installed packages ship, and `read_scale("carriers")` opens
  the one the core ships: the energypal fuel taxonomy with the IPCC 2006
  default calorific values and CO2 factors (`?shipped_scales`).

### Dimension packages

* [timescales](https://github.com/optimal2050/timescales): `Calendar`, a
  nested scale of time. A catalog of standard calendars, construction from
  tokens, conversion from datetimes, sampled and fiscal calendars, calendar
  plots.
* [geoscales](https://github.com/optimal2050/geoscales): `GeoScale`, a
  nested scale of space. Region hierarchies from data providers, geometry
  and area weights, maps.
* The *Building a dimension package* section of the reference lists the
  hooks a subclass fills, including how it stores and restores its payload
  in a definition file.

Both are designed for optimization and simulation models, where the labelled
time slices and regions become the index sets of variables and constraints
(see [energyRt](https://github.com/optimal2050/energyRt)).

## Planned

The order is not fixed; items move up as the modelling packages need them.

* **User-defined transition rules.** Today a rule is one of the seven names.
  A registered rule will also be able to be a function of the values and
  weights in a group, so a dimension or a model can define its own
  aggregation (a maximum, a quantile, a nonlinear combination).
* **Joint weights on products.** `ScaleProduct` reserves `joint_weights`
  for a weight that varies across axes together (an hourly profile that
  differs by region). The slot is validated but not yet used by
  `recast_product()`.
* **Residual protection across scales.** Declared residuals are protected
  when disaggregating within one scale; the cross-scale route does not yet
  apply it.
* **Visualization in the core.** Plots live in the dimension packages
  (calendar heat maps, choropleths). A dimension-free layout of a scale's
  structure -- icicle and stacked views of levels and shares -- belongs in
  the core, so any dimension can be drawn and the dimension packages can
  build on it.
* **Scales from continuous variables.** Income brackets, temperature
  regimes and vintage bins are nested scales whose atoms are intervals of a
  continuous variable. Today they are binned by hand before
  `scale_from_leaftable()`; a constructor taking breakpoints, with the
  interval bounds kept as weights, would build them directly.
* **More shipped definitions.** `carriers` is the first classification the
  core ships. Industry classifications (NACE, ISIC) and technology vintages
  follow as definition files under `inst/scales/`, moving to a separate
  data package only if their size demands it. Regional values of an
  attribute (a national calorific value) belong to a product of the scale
  with a `GeoScale`, attached under their own source; not built yet.

## Not planned

* Trees as node objects, or an object per unit. The flat atom table is the
  representation, and it is what keeps conversion the same for every
  dimension.
* Guessing a rule when none is given. A value column with no rule is an
  error; a silently chosen rule is a silent unit error.
